items.label: A
items.critique: Practical, scene-bound briefing that names the spells it hands over and why (invisibility for guards), with the stock 'Good luck and good speed'. Plain and slightly clumsy in a Westwood way.

items.label: B
items.critique: Tidy cause-and-effect exposition (tower, road, harvest, therefore the Ogre Lord) that over-explains the stakes; 'in their claws' and the neat staging at the north gate feel composed rather than blurted.

items.label: C
items.critique: Stiff, fragmentary self-introduction ('The Master for the [Place].'), capitalised 'YOU', and a reminder that restates the stakes instead of the task: Westwood's awkward plainness.

items.label: D
items.critique: Double-dash aside, 'darkest hour', 'She knows you are coming', and the one-line dramatic page '[Place] has no one else.' are modern cinematic beats; the reminder 'Enough idle talk' is generic.

items.label: E
items.critique: Carefully paced short pages with a homely hand-off and a gifted sword; flavour lines ('come sniffing', 'feel its edge', 'Mind your step') are polished atmosphere Westwood rarely spends on an opener.

items.label: F
items.critique: Exclamatory, slightly silly mayor with 'nettlesome urchins', explicit directions ('East of here', 'house at the center of town'), odd capitalisation of Urchins: classic Nox.

items.label: G
items.critique: Breathless shouting with '!?', run-on exclamations and awkward 'leaving rebuilding the village our smallest concern' - the overwrought but plain Westwood panic voice with a clear destination.

items.label: H
items.critique: Opening starts mid-thought and the reminder repeats itself; the joke 'you'll smell him before you see him' and the rigged-rockfall warning read like a modern writer's scouting brief.

tells: Westwood's openings are clumsy and literal: fragments, odd capitalisation, '!?', all-caps emphasis, and stakes restated bluntly; the new texts are smoother and more evenly paced.
New texts lean on cinematic dramatic beats (short isolated pages like 'X has no one else.', 'She knows you are coming', 'darkest hour') and on double-dash asides, which Westwood does not use.

New texts over-explain causal logic and add homely flavour verbs ('come sniffing', 'in their claws', 'feel its edge'); Westwood gives the task and, when a tool is handed over, says exactly what it is for.
Westwood reminders often comment on the situation or repeat the stakes; new reminders tend to be brisk 'Off with you, go!' shoos or redundant restatements of the task.
